summary: SELENE Horizon is an interactive web application designed to evaluate, visualise and compare solar illumination conditions, electrical power generation potential and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows across the lunar south pole.
details:
System Architecture & How It Works

The system translates astrodynamic and topographic calculations into a streamlined three-layer pipeline:

- Selection & Parameterization Layer (Frontend): Users can choose from six pre-configured landing sites of high scientific and engineering interest or input custom topocentric coordinates (latitude and longitude), along with a custom mission time window (Start Time and Stop Time).

- Ephemeris & Topographic Data Engine (Backend / API Integration): Built with Python and FastAPI, the backend orchestrates requests to NASA's open data services:

  • JPL Horizons API: Queries topocentric observer ephemerides for locations on the lunar surface, simultaneously tracking the Sun and Earth. Apparent azimuth and elevation data are retrieved and parsed from the ephemeris.
  • LOLA Elevation Data (self-hosted): Lunar topographic elevation data from LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) measurements, sourced from PGDA and served locally to ensure operation without venue network connectivity. This terrain model is used to calculate local horizon profiles and identify potential obstructions.

- Engineering Processing & Visualization:

  • Dual-Scale Topographic Visualization: The lunar terrain and horizon geometry are represented through two complementary visual perspectives:
  • Regional Polar Overview (Zenithal View): A top-down map of the lunar polar region, based on NASA topographic data, showing the spatial distribution of selected landing sites within the broader south-polar terrain. This view provides geographic context and allows users to identify the relationship between candidate locations and surrounding topographic features.
  • Site-Specific Horizon Panorama (360° Skyline View): For each selected site, the backend derives an azimuth-dependent terrain horizon profile from the LOLA elevation model. Displayed as a panoramic skyline, this representation maps the local terrain elevation angle against azimuth (0°–360°), revealing crater rims, ridges, and other potential obstructions around the observer. The apparent trajectories of the Sun and Earth can then be overlaid on this profile to visualize when each body rises above or falls below the local terrain horizon.
  • Topographic Horizon Masking: By comparing the apparent elevation of the Sun and Earth against the corresponding terrain horizon angles, the engine determines terrain-aware geometric visibility rather than relying solely on a smooth-sphere approximation. Angular margins can also be considered to account for the apparent size of the solar disk and communication-link clearance criteria.
  • Power & Link Computation: Calculates cumulative solar energy yield in kWh/m² based on effective illumination intervals and solar irradiance, alongside Earth line-of-sight availability over the selected mission window.
Key Benefits
  • Scientific Precision with Intuitive UX: Abstracts complex parameter configurations and raw ephemeris and topographic datasets into an immediate, visual workflow, making the underlying astrodynamic and terrain calculations accessible.
  • Multi-Scale Terrain Awareness: Combines a regional zenithal view of the lunar south pole with site-specific 360° horizon panoramas. Users can move from the broader geographic context to the local skyline that directly determines solar and Earth visibility.
  • Terrain-Aware Mission Realism: Integrating LOLA topography captures crater-rim shadowing and mountain obstructions, avoiding false-positive sunlight or communication estimates associated with simplified spherical-horizon models.
  • Actionable Engineering Trade-offs: Enables instant comparison between contrasting operational profiles—such as maximizing continuous solar power generation on the Shackleton–de Gerlache Connecting Ridge versus maintaining near-uninterrupted Earth line-of-sight on Malapert Massif.
  • Educational & Public Accessibility: Makes complex orbital geometry, including lunar libration and polar grazing sunlight, easier to explore for students, educators, and the public.
